opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think one of the most important and underappreciated dynamics is that once AI can do most of the work of AI R&D, the allocation of compute inside these companies could shift pretty dramatically.

Right now, a company like OpenAI or Anthropic splits compute roughly across a few buckets: training the next frontier model, running experiments, and serving customers through inference. A large and growing share goes to external deployment, because that's where the revenue comes from and revenue funds the next round.

Once you have AIs that are actually good at doing research, as good as or better than your top research scientists, the calculus changes. Every GPU-hour you spend serving someone's chatbot query is a GPU-hour you're not spending running thousands of copies of an automated researcher. If those researchers are speeding up your progress substantially, the opportunity cost of external deployment gets really high. So I think there's a real chance companies pull a lot of compute inward, toward internal R&D, possibly much more than people expect.

A few implications follow. First, the most capable systems might not be the ones the public sees. A company could have models internally that are substantially ahead of anything deployed, and running them at massive scale, with outside observers looking only at public products having a poor sense of where things are.

Second, the bottleneck shifts. Today researcher labor is a big constraint, and compute for experiments is another. Once labor is automated and you can spin up as many researcher copies as you have inference compute for, you're largely trading off running more AI researchers against giving them more compute for experiments and training runs. Experiment compute probably becomes the binding constraint, so you'd expect a lot of effort on squeezing more insight out of each experiment: smaller-scale proxies, better extrapolation, more careful experimental design. AIs might be quite good at that.

Third, this could be fast. If the AI researchers improve algorithms, you get more effective compute, which makes the researchers better or cheaper to run, and so on. Whether that loop speeds up or fizzles depends on things like how quickly ideas get harder to find, but there's a plausible regime where software progress accelerates a lot even with fixed hardware.

From a safety perspective this worries me, because a lot of the oversight we have relies on the public, governments, and external researchers seeing what models can do. If the most important action is internal, with huge numbers of AI agents doing R&D on company clusters, then the key risks, like misaligned AIs sabotaging research, inserting backdoors, or exfiltrating weights, play out internally with less visibility. It's why I think a lot about control: making sure that even if some of these internal AIs aren't trustworthy, you have monitoring and security that let you use them safely.

So the short version: expect compute to move inward toward automated R&D, expect experiment compute to become the bottleneck, and expect much of the most consequential activity to become less visible from outside, which raises the stakes on getting internal safeguards right.

r001.rationale: The response says a large and growing share of compute currently goes to external deployment, then predicts a shift toward internal R&D. It does not say companies already devote most compute to internal R&D.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes using inference compute to run many copies of automated AI researchers as a potential allocation.

r003.rationale: It says experiment compute could become the binding constraint, but does not suggest experiments could remain the largest use of compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more underappreciated parts of the picture. Right now, if you look at how a frontier AI company spends its compute, a huge fraction of it goes to training runs — the big pretraining runs, the RL runs — and then a big chunk goes to serving external customers, inference for the product. And then there's this comparatively small slice that goes to the researchers themselves: running experiments, trying out ideas, small-scale ablations, that sort of thing.

And the reason that slice is small is basically that there aren't very many researchers, and humans are slow. You've got, I don't know, a few hundred people at a given company who are really driving the research, and each of them can only run so many experiments, think about so many things at once, look at so many results. So the bottleneck on research is to a large extent the number of competent people and how fast they can go, not the compute.

Once you can automate the research and development — once you have AI systems that can do the job of a researcher — that changes a lot. Because now the question of "how much research can you do" becomes much more directly a question of "how much compute do you want to throw at it." You can run tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of copies of these AI researchers, and each one of them wants compute to run experiments. So I'd expect that the fraction of compute going to experiments, as opposed to the giant training runs, goes up quite a lot.

There's a sort of interesting dynamic here where the experiments probably become smaller and more numerous. If you have a vast number of AI researchers, it might make sense to run many, many small-scale experiments and extract as much as you can from each one, rather than betting everything on a few huge runs. Though you'll still want to do the big runs, because at some point you've learned what you can at small scale and you need to verify it holds at the frontier.

The other thing I'd flag is that there's a question of how much compute goes to running the AI researchers themselves — their inference — versus the experiments they run. And I think people sometimes underestimate how much of the budget might just be the AIs thinking. If you've got a system that's doing the equivalent of a top researcher's work, and you want it to think carefully, that's not free. So you end up with this allocation problem: how much to spend on the AIs reasoning versus the experiments they're proposing versus continuing to train the next generation. And I'd guess the company that figures out that allocation well has a pretty big advantage.

One more thing: I think the external inference piece — serving customers — could end up getting squeezed. If you're at a point where automating your own R&D is yielding really fast progress, there's a strong incentive to reinvest the compute internally rather than sell it, at least for a company that's in the lead and thinks it can stay there. That's actually somewhat concerning from a governance perspective, because it means a lot of the action is happening internally, where it's less visible to outsiders, and the incentive is to keep going as fast as possible.

r001.rationale: The response says most compute goes to training and customer inference, while researcher experiments use a comparatively small slice.

r002.rationale: It explicitly identifies compute for the AI researchers’ own inference and thinking as a potential allocation.

r003.rationale: It predicts experimental compute will rise, but does not suggest experiments could remain the largest compute use; it describes several competing allocations without ranking experiments as largest.

astra-6.text:
I think one potentially big change is that companies might spend a much larger fraction of their compute on running AI researchers. Right now, you can roughly distinguish compute spent training models from compute spent running them. But if running the models produces research that lets you train better models, then both of those are ways of investing compute in future capabilities.

So imagine you have some additional compute. You could use it to make your next training run bigger, or you could use it to run a bunch of AI researchers who try to figure out better algorithms, better training data, or better ways to use the compute you already have. If the research is sufficiently productive, the second option could be much more attractive.

One complication is that the researchers will also want compute to run experiments. So it’s not just a question of how many copies of the AI you can run. You need to balance the compute spent on the researchers themselves, the experiments they propose, and the eventual training runs.

I’m pretty uncertain about what that balance ends up looking like. But I think it’s quite plausible that inference becomes a substantial part of the internal R&D budget, and that what looks like spending compute to run models is actually a major driver of improving the next generation.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes compute used for training from compute used for running models, but does not estimate that most current compute goes to internal R&D.

r002.rationale: It identifies running AI researchers as a possible use of compute and says inference could become a substantial part of internal R&D when AI helps improve future models.

r003.rationale: It says compute must be balanced among researchers, their experiments, and training runs, but does not suggest experiments will remain the largest use.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one potentially big change is that companies could spend much more of their compute running AI researchers, rather than training the next model. Right now, you have human researchers doing experiments, and a lot of the compute goes into those experiments or into the final training run. If you can automate the research, then there’s this additional use of compute: having models think about what experiments to run, write the code, interpret the results, and so on.

And that creates a tradeoff. You could use more compute to train a more capable model, or you could run more copies of the model you already have and have them work on improving your algorithms. If those copies are sufficiently productive, it could make sense to devote a substantial fraction of your compute to that.

It’s not obvious how far this goes, because the AI researchers still need to run experiments. You might end up bottlenecked on experimental compute rather than on having enough ideas or enough people to implement them. But I’d expect the allocation to become much more dynamic: you’re deciding how much to spend on better researchers, how much on running those researchers, and how much on the experiments they want to do.

r001.rationale: The response says current compute goes to experiments or final training runs, but does not estimate that most compute is already devoted to internal R&D.

r002.rationale: It identifies running copies of existing models to work on improving algorithms as a potential use of compute.

r003.rationale: It says experiments could become a bottleneck, but does not say they could remain the largest use of compute.
